source_text:
Nec de fato quisquam aut solacium captet aut excuseteuentum: sit sors fortunae, mens tamen libera est, et ideo actus hominis, non dignitas iudicatur.
quid enim aliud est fatum quam quod de unoquoque nostrum Deus fatus est ? qui cum possit praescire materiam, pro meritis et qualitatibus singulorum etiam fata determinat. ita in nobis non genitura plectitur, sed ingenii natura punitur. ac de fato satis, uel si pauca pro tempore, disputaturi alias et uberius et plenius.
ceterum quod plerique pauperes dicimur, non est infamia nostra, sed gloria: animus enim ut luxu soluitur, ita frugalitate firmatur.
et tamen qui potest pauper esse qui non eget, qui non inhiat alieno, qui Deo diues est? magis pauper ille est, qui cum multa habeat, plura desiderat.
dicam tamen quemadmodum sentio: nemo tam pauper potest esse quam natus est. aues sine patrimonio uiuunt et in diem pascuntur: et haec nobis tamen nata sunt, quae omnia, si non concupiscimus, possidemus.
igitur ut qui uiam terit, eo felicior quo leuior incedit, ita beatior in hoc itinere uiuendi, qui paupertate se subleuat, non sub diuitiarum onere suspirat.
et tamen facultates, si utiles putaremus, a Deo posceremus: utique indulgere posset aliquantum ■ cuius est totum. sed nos contemnere malumus opes quam contingere, innocentiam magis cupimus, magis patientiam flagitamus, malumus nos bonos esse quam prodigos, et quod corporis humana uitia sentimus et patimur, non est poena, militia est.
fortitudo enim in infirmitatibus roboratur et calamitas saepius disciplina uirtutis est. uires denique et mentis et corporis sine laboris exercitatione torpescunt: omnes adeo uestri uiri fortes, quos in exemplum praedicatis, aerumnis suis inclyti floruerunt.
itaque et nobis Deus nec non potest subuenire nec despicit, cum sit et omnium rector et amator suorum, sed in aduersis unumquemque explorat et examinat, ingenium singulorum periculis pensitat, usque ad extremam mortem uoluntatem hominis sciscitatur, nihil sibi posse perire securus. itaque ut aurum ignibus, sic nos discriminibus arguimur.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians are poor and miserable, explaining that fate is God's decree, poverty is no disgrace, and hardships are God's testing of his own.
pass_a_gloss: And let no one either seek comfort from fate or excuse the outcome: let the lot be of fortune, yet the mind is free, and therefore the act of a human being, not his rank, is judged. For what else is fate than what God has spoken about each one of us? Since he is able to know the material beforehand, he also determines fates according to the merits and qualities of individuals. Thus in us not the birth is punished, but the nature of the character is punished. And about fate enough, even if few things for the present time, since we will dispute at another time both more fully and more completely. But as for the fact that most of us are called poor, it is not our disgrace, but our glory: for the mind, just as it is weakened by luxury, so it is strengthened by frugality. And yet who can be poor who does not lack, who does not gape after another's property, who is rich in God? More poor is that man who, though he has many things, desires more. I will say nevertheless what I feel: no one can be as poor as he was born. Birds live without an inheritance and are fed for the day: and yet these things were born for us, all of which, if we do not covet them, we possess. Therefore just as he who treads a road is the happier the lighter he walks, so in this journey of living he is more blessed who lifts himself up by poverty, who does not sigh under the burden of riches. And yet riches, if we thought them useful, we would ask from God: indeed he could grant somewhat, whose is the whole. But we prefer to despise wealth than to touch it, we desire innocence more, we demand patience more, we prefer to be good than lavish, and the fact that we feel and suffer the human defects of the body is not punishment, it is military service. For strength is made strong in weaknesses, and calamity is more often the training of virtue. Finally the powers both of mind and of body grow sluggish without the exercise of labor: all your brave men, whom you proclaim as examples, flourished famous through their own hardships. And so God both can help us and does not despise us, since he is both the ruler of all things and the lover of his own, but in adversities he tests and examines each one, he weighs the character of individuals by dangers, he inquires into the will of a man up to the final death, secure that nothing of his can perish. Therefore just as gold is proved by fires, so we are proved by critical moments.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'fate' for fatum, and Octavius is redefining it as God's decree.
The metaphor of Christian suffering as military service is central to Octavius's argument and recurs in the following section.
Discrimen here means a decisive test or crisis, matching the metaphor of gold proved by fire.
Ingenium here means innate character or disposition, contrasted with genitura (birth).
This preserves the paradox of Christian wealth in God, which is the point of the rhetorical question.

pass_b_english: No one should seek comfort or excuse for his conduct in fate. Let a person's lot be whatever fortune wills, but the mind remains free, and so it is a man's action that is judged, not his station.

For what else is fate than what God has spoken concerning each one of us? Since he can know the material beforehand, he determines our fates according to the merits and qualities of each individual. Thus it is not our birth that is punished in us, but the nature of our character. And enough about fate, even if briefly for the present; we will discuss it more fully and completely another time.

As for the fact that most of us are called poor, that is not our disgrace but our glory. The mind is loosened by luxury, just as it is strengthened by frugality. And yet who can be poor if he lacks nothing, does not gape after another's goods, and is rich in God? That man is poorer who, though he has much, desires more.

I will tell you what I think: no one can be as poor as he was when he was born. Birds live without an inheritance and are fed day by day; and all these things were made for us, and if we do not covet them, we possess them.

Therefore, just as a man who travels a road is happier the lighter he walks, so in this journey of life the man is more blessed who lifts himself up by poverty and does not sigh under the burden of riches.

And yet if we thought wealth useful, we would ask it from God. Surely he to whom the whole belongs could grant us some portion. But we prefer to despise riches rather than to grasp them; we desire innocence more, we more urgently seek patience; we prefer to be good rather than extravagant.

And the human weaknesses of the body that we feel and suffer are not punishment; it is service as soldiers. For courage is strengthened in infirmities, and calamity is often the training ground of virtue. In fact, the powers of both mind and body grow sluggish without the exercise of labor. All your brave men, whom you praise as examples, flourished and became famous through their hardships.

So God both can help us and does not despise us, since he is the ruler of all things and the lover of his own. But in adversity he tests and examines each one; he weighs the character of individuals through dangers; he inquires into a man's will even to his final death, certain that nothing of his can perish. Therefore, as gold is proved by fire, so we are proved by critical moments.

problems.why: flagitamus means we urgently request/beg for, not 'demand' in the sense of requiring as a right; in Christian Latin this is prayer language, not demanding.
problems.ruling: source "magis patientiam flagitamus" = we earnestly beg/long for patience; "demand" misstates tone.

fixed: Changed 'we demand patience more' to 'we more urgently seek patience': flagitamus means to beg or urgently request, not to demand as a right, and in Christian Latin it is prayer language.

problems.why: "Militia" means service/soldiery metaphorically, not literal military service; the sense is "it is service/service as a soldier" or "it is our campaign/struggle".
problems.fix: it is our service as soldiers, not punishment
problems.ruling: "militia est" is metaphorical (service/discipline), not literal military service.

fixed: Changed 'it is military service' to 'it is service as soldiers' because the source 'militia est' is metaphorical for service or soldiery, not literal military service.

last_rejected.why: militia means military service/service, not "service as soldiers" with its modern connotation
last_rejected.fix: it is not punishment but service
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'militia' = military service; translation 'service as soldiers' conveys same sense, not a meaning change

polish.changed: Clarified that Octavius is the speaker throughout, smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud, and kept every claim and qualification intact.

notes.quote: blind fortune or uncertain nature rules
notes.why: These terms shift between Caecilius's skeptical 'fortune/nature' and Octavius's theological 'fate' without clear distinction of who uses which.
notes.fix: Clarify that 'fate' is God's ordering, 'fortune' is blind chance.

notes.quote: For what else is fate than what God has spoken concerning each one of us?
notes.why: Octavius redefines 'fate' as divine decree, but this contradicts earlier distinction between fate and providence.
notes.fix: Note: Stoic-Christian synthesis, redefining pagan terms.
